plain: Wispr Flow is an AI dictation app. The idea is simple: you place the cursor where you'd normally type, you talk, and Flow turns your voice into clean text right inside that same application. It's not n8n, it doesn't run workflows and it doesn't decide anything for you. Its value is removing the typing bottleneck: emails, prompts, notes, messages, short documentation, and first drafts of ideas that come out better spoken than typed.

account.free: The official site lets you start for free and shows availability for Mac, Windows, iPhone, and Android. Before relying on the tool for real work, check the pricing page for your plan's limits, what features it includes, and how it handles voice data.
steps: Use the official site. From there you can download the app or see the options available for your device.
Install the app on your device
Choose Mac, Windows, iPhone, or Android depending on where you type most. On mobile it works as a keyboard or voice input; on desktop it works over whichever fields you already type in.
No microphone, no dictation. Only grant it once you understand when it's listening and how it stops.
Do a test in an empty note
Don't start with a real email. Open a note, talk for twenty seconds, and see what it does with pauses, punctuation, names, and technical terms.
Learn the start and stop gesture
The tool depends on controlling when it's listening. Practice starting, pausing, canceling, and reviewing before using it with clients.
Check whether it stores learning of names or jargon, whether you can delete data, and whether there's a team or enterprise policy.
account.warning: Don't dictate sensitive data in shared spaces or transcribe other people's conversations without permission. In Spain and the EU, voice, names, clients, and meetings can involve personal data.

first: Open an empty note and dictate a disorganized idea for twenty seconds. The goal is to see how it cleans up filler words and punctuates, not to write it perfectly.
Repeat the same idea in a test email or chat to check whether it works the same inside another app.
Dictate three proper names, a brand, and a technical term from your work. Check whether it understands them or you have to correct them.
Try dictating a prompt for ChatGPT: speak the full brief and then only fix the gaps between brackets.
Note when it saves you time and when it doesn't. If the text requires exact formatting, code, or critical figures, the keyboard might still be better.
shortcuts: The main action. Used to start talking right where the cursor is and stop when the idea is done.
Necessary if you spoke wrong, there was noise, or you said something you don't want left written.
Flow leaves the text much cleaner than a literal transcript, but proper names, figures, URLs, and technical terms always need reviewing.
Some versions learn names, jargon, and preferences. Use it to reduce corrections, not to feed in sensitive information without thinking.
The point is you don't have to copy and paste: you talk in Gmail, Slack, WhatsApp, ChatGPT, Docs, or wherever the cursor is.
Check the language before a long session. Mixing languages while talking can work, but it should always be reviewed before sending.
daily: Use it for fast first drafts: ideas, replies, your own meeting notes, prompts, and short documentation.
Speak in short sentences. You don't need to sound like a news anchor; you do need to finish one idea before jumping to the next.
Always review before sending. Dictating fast and sending without looking just swaps one bottleneck for another.
Don't use it as a secret recorder. If someone else is talking, ask permission and explain what the text will be used for.
Have a backup plan: if there's noise, bad connection, unusual names, or important figures, go back to the keyboard.
The best test is measuring real time: write a normal reply with the keyboard, then dictate it, and compare quality and minutes.
errors: The text comes out well written but doesn't say exactly what I wanted
You spoke too abstractly. Repeat it with a structure: context, decision, details, and closing. Then review before sending.
Proper names or technical terms come out wrong
Dictate them slowly the first time, correct the text, and check whether the tool learns that word. If it's a critical piece of data, type it by hand.
It punctuates strangely or merges sentences that were separate
Make clearer pauses and dictate shorter sentences. If formatting matters, review it in a note before pasting it into the final destination.
Check system permissions, the selected microphone, and whether another app is using it. Test in an empty note before blaming the document.
I feel embarrassed talking to the computer
Start by dictating only private notes. Practice changes the feeling fast, but not every task and every place is good for voice.
words: Talking in order to write. It's not a call or a long recording: it's swapping the keyboard for voice for a few seconds.
The conversion of what you say into written words. The AI improves punctuation and clarity so it doesn't read like a raw transcript.
Where the cursor is. Flow writes there: a note, an email, a chat, or a prompt box.
Words like um, well, so. The tool usually cleans them up, but it doesn't fix an idea that isn't fully thought through yet.
Names, brands, and terms you repeat. If it learns them, you correct less; if they're sensitive, think before dictating them.
Authorization to listen. You should know when it's active and how to turn it off.
matters: Knowing how to start and stop without overthinking it. If the gesture isn't automatic, you won't use it when you're in a hurry.
Reviewing names, figures, links, and technical terms. These are the four spots where an almost-correct sentence can cause a problem.
Using it for long prompts. Speaking the full context is usually faster than typing a poor one-line brief.
Keeping dictation separate from automation. Wispr Flow writes; it doesn't trigger workflows, doesn't send messages on its own, and doesn't replace a designed process.
Checking privacy before dictating content about clients, students, or meetings.
ignore: Looking for twenty automations inside Wispr Flow. It's not that kind of tool.
Expecting it to leave a legal text, a figure, or code perfect without human review.
Using it in noisy places or in front of people who don't know you're dictating work information.
Comparing it to n8n, Zapier, or Make. Flow improves text input; those tools run processes.

usage.unit: words dictated, minutes of voice, and plan limits
usage.explanation: Measure Wispr Flow by time saved and accuracy, not by number of workflows. Do a test with three kinds of text: a private note, a test email, and a long prompt. Note how long it takes, how many corrections you make, and whether the result can be sent after reviewing.
examples: A twenty-second note with a disorganized idea.
A five-line test email, reviewed before sending.
A long prompt dictated inside ChatGPT or Claude.
The correction rate on names, figures, and technical terms.
The date you checked your plan, privacy, and supported devices.
